I don't know if this is a common thing, if this is all — you know, but there’s a lot of things that we gotta look at. The only reason — and the other thing; those of you that do the job, I would never charge you with a crime and let it continue — I don't have the ability to dismiss it, but I can work with the county attorney and those type of things. But at the end of the day, if we believe that it truly needs to go away, it’ll go away. But I guess I just wanted to stop and let you guys know that we do appreciate you and what you're doing, and it is a needed — what you do is very needed. I couldn't do it. I don't know how to do this stuff. I rely on you folks to help us. The two gentlemen that night, they're good guys, but you gotta understand that when you come here in rural Iowa from Florida, you're from Seattle, Washington, chances of you coming back when I ask you to come back and answer questions are slim to none, I promise you that. So, we just — I just met you, so you're not gonna — there’s a whole lot of questions that go into these things in the middle of the night that we have to — we have to put all that together. So, I just wanted to stop and tell you that there is no friction between — as far as I’m concerned, between us. Just asking that you kinda wait for it. We're not out to prosecute anybody. I would never charge any one of you with a crime if I didn't think it was valid. If it’s proven down the road and if we get through this investigation with all these other agencies and it needs to go away, I’ll advocate for it to go away. I wouldn't want any one of you to have a criminal history that you didn't deserve. So, if I could recommend anything, it would be work with your local law enforcement when you're doing it. I would have helped. If I would have known about it, I would have helped you do it. You know, I would have helped them accomplish their mission that night, so — and we wouldn't have any of these problems. So — but anyway. JACK: I think Awareness Con did, in fact, change the hearts and minds of those living in Iowa, because after that there was much more support for these two penetration testers who got arrested. They were starting to come around and feel sorry for them. Some were even saying, please don't judge Iowa based on this. So, while I was at DEFCON, I ran into those two penetration testers from this Iowa County Courthouse story, and it’s now been six years since this happened and we last spoke. So, I wanted to get together with them and find a spot at DEFCON and sit down and hear what’s new. [To guests] So, you got arrested, got your charges, got the charges dropped. Story’s over, right? Anything else happen since then? GABBY: A couple things. JACK: What’s new with you? GABBY: I mean, so, have you ever heard that thing where like — you go to prison and you turn gay? Yeah, I’m not gay, but definitely turned into a girl. JACK: Gary has changed her name to Gabby. GABBY: Well, it’s my handle. I just, I guess, absorbed the handle Gabby, yeah, 'cause I can — like to be anyone I want to be. JACK: You got your charges dropped. So, after charges are dropped, are you like, I’m good? Like, I can finally go back to my life, everything is fine. GABBY: I don't feel like it was like that at all because there was so many things they said that just were not accurate or just outward lies, fabrications like changing the narrative just to say, oh, cool, we're innocent. Well, no shit. Obviously we're innocent the entire time, which is why we never settled for anything the entire time. So, them dropping it would almost be like them doing us a favor, which was not the case. They did themselves no favors by dropping it other than embarrassing themselves further. That was for them, definitely not for us. JACK: Well, what more can you do after charges are dropped? GABBY: That’s part of the judicial system that’s messed up, is you're guilty until proven innocent. You spend time in jail, you get your name dragged through the mud, they lie about everything, and then there’s zero repercussions unless you go after them for a personal suit. JACK: [Music] A personal lawsuit, is that possible? Can you sue for wrongful arrest? They felt like something seriously unjust happened to them, and they wanted to do something to make it right. JUSTIN: I think Gabby was already thinking about you looking at her mugshot, smiling in there. She was already thinking about the lawsuit as soon as the cuffs went on. GABBY: Pretty much. JACK: You were in the jail cells saying, as soon as I get outta here I’m gonna sue these guys. GABBY: Oh, my — 'cause I knew we had done — we were the most cooperative — at least one of us was for 99% of the time. The other was 100%. But again, you had nothing wrong with what you did. They were being super invasive. JUSTIN: Oh, I don't trust them to give me my information. I saw how they secure things. GABBY: But that was — it’s a good learning point, right? Because we're like, we did nothing wrong. We're gonna be completely cooperative. We're gonna do everything, and then you do everything right, and then they just lie about stuff to try to cover their own butt and to try to make it look like they didn't do anything wrong. You're like, wait a minute, I was truthful, I was honest, I cooperated with you guys and then you turn around and you completely spin the narrative so you don't get in trouble or you don't look bad or to save your job or whatever it is. So, not cooperating to me sounds like the right choice after going through that. JACK: Suing the sheriff felt like the right choice for them, making him pay for the wrongs that he’s caused, expose the errors in his ways, make him the guilty one. But to conduct a lawsuit such as this, it was going to cost a lot of time and a lot of money. GABBY: We actually had our original lawyer and we asked him. Like, I think we would really like to go after the county and the state and the sheriff, because people need to know that this is not okay. Like, they just can't get away with stuff like this. He had a real — he was afraid to do it, for lack of a better term, because he’s like, this is small-town Iowa. It’s not big. Everybody knows who I am, and I feel like if I go after the county and the state and the sheriff and all these lawmakers, especially after they had that investigation — and he’s like, I don't know that that would be great for my career at all. JACK: So, their lawyer made a few phone calls and found them another lawyer named Marty who was just about to retire. GABBY: He’s a civil rights lawyer and he loved the case. He’s like, I will take it on. I’ll do it pro bono. He’s like, I’ve made my money. Like, I — he’s literally at the twilight of his career. He extended his career to finish this case. JACK: So, they got a new lawyer, and they wanted to sue the sheriff, the prosecutor, the judge, all these people who treated them bad. But this is where Gabby and Justin started learning some new words, words like… GABBY: Qualified immunity. JACK: And sovereign immunity. See, qualified immunity means you can't sue government workers, especially judges, prosecutors, and cops. They're shielded by the government itself. So, they can't sue the actual people who did them wrong, who made these mistakes. Then there’s sovereign immunity, which means you can't sue the government unless the government agrees to be sued. GABBY: Well, we tried to go after the state, and it’s very convoluted because the state is the one that passes judgment on whether or not the state is guilty or not. So, it’s like somebody coming to you and saying, we're gonna sue you. Are you guilty? You're like, of course I’m not. They're like, oh, sorry, can't sue you now because you said I’m — I said I’m not guilty. So, the state immediately threw it out. JACK: They tried to make this a federal case to sue the state. Since the state wouldn't pick it up, maybe the federal government could oversee it and decide. It got picked up by a federal court, but then when they looked at it, they just kicked it back down to the state, who just closed it right away. GABBY: So, it’s just like, they tried so hard to stack the deck against us at the — at every single turn just to make it where it was not going to be or didn't feel like it was impartial at all through the entire process. Like, every step they could take to stack the deck in their favor, they absolutely tried to do and absolutely did. JACK: So, this lawsuit they wanted to wage was dead in the water before it even got a chance to begin, which is really frustrating because what mechanism can you even use here to bring justice to a situation like this? GABBY: So, we were left with the county and the sheriff. So, even though the sheriff has qualified immunity — or the prosecutor is the one; the prosecutor is the one that has qualified immunity. The sheriff has some protections, but not complete. So, we had to go through the process of saying, these are all the things that we think he did wrong, and then the judge said, yes, yes, no, no, no. Then we eventually are left with what the lawsuit ended up — and so, they said there is enough evidence to show that the sheriff did do these things wrong. So, we were able to go after the sheriff, but we went after the sheriff’s position, not Chad Leonard the person. So, we had to go after the actual sheriff, which means he’s also covered by the county’s insurance policy, and nothing, not one cent comes out of his pocket. He doesn't get reprimand — like, nothing, absolutely nothing happens to him. It’s a moral victory at best. JACK: Okay, so they started a single lawsuit that got accepted in the courts against the county and the sheriff’s position. Finally this thing was starting to get some traction, and this felt like progress since Justin and Gabby really wanted to use the system to seek justice of everything that went wrong. [To guests] Now, my question is, what were you hoping to get out of the lawsuit? GABBY: One dollar. JACK: One dollar? GABBY: That was all I cared about. I told…   I was like, as long as I can drag this dude through the mud like he did with us except with facts instead of stories, that’s all I care about, which is — the entire time, which is why we were like — they were like, you should just take the trespassing charge, and — nope, nope, nope, the entire time. My entire goal was just to show that this — show this person for who he really was, which is just a lying, corrupt individual. JACK: Dang, this is getting pretty good. They got a lawyer who’s all in, retired, working for free, doesn't care about what people think of him anymore, and Gabby’s just coming out with claws out. This is gonna be a good fight. They eventually decided to ask for more than a dollar. They wanted this to hurt, and they also wanted to cause panic and fear within the county, and they also wanted the townspeople to see what happens when you elect a corrupt sheriff. JUSTIN: We submitted the maximum amount that the insurance company would have covered for the county. So, we didn’t want taxpayers having to front more money for having a poorly-elected sheriff. So, yeah, that’s the dollar amount that we set. I think the other part of it, too, that’s really important, what we wanted out of the case was to set new precedent, that this isn't okay. You can't put hackers in jail and try to prosecute them when you hired them to help defend you. JACK: So, they were now seeking quite a bit of money from this lawsuit. I’m not sure exactly how much; they wouldn't tell me. My guess is that they wanted to split $1 million. Keep in mind, they already paid $50,000 each just to get out on bail, and then they spent the night in jail, and they were threatened with seven years of prison that — they had to fight tooth and nail to get that charge dropped. Those lawyer fees added up, too, of course. That’s a lot of stress, real costs, and anguish that they had to go through. So, to split $1 million, I think that sounds reasonable for the amount of hardship they endured. But Gabby was still furious from this whole ordeal. GABBY: Like World War II, the — what’s the saying? They woke the sleeping giant. Japan thought if they came in and they smashed us that we would back off and just slink away and not do anything. Kinda the same thing here where, oh, if we just throw our weight around and we threaten these guys with six years in prison and all this other stuff, they’ll just take the deal and they’ll go away, and that was not the case. We don't fuck up. Justin and I, we do things by the letter, by the contract. Everything we do is meticulously perfect for that reason, because of what we do. We don't want to mess up. I think all that — this whole thing just showed that and highlighted it, because if we had done something wrong, they would have found it, and they were unable to. So now, five years later, the tables had turned, and we had all the evidence. We had all the data. We had the video cameras and we had the recordings and we had everything. [Music] Then it was the exact opposite, where the county and the state was like, oh shit, they've got everything and we literally have nothing except a really, really bad arrest from a corrupt individual. JACK: Together they had collected tons of evidence supporting their case, and they were feeding it to the court, and the county was starting to sweat a little. Despite how confident Gabby felt that they would win this case, it’s still a scary thing to go up against the government. I mean, they could drag this case on for years and exhaust you and run you dry of money and energy, only to ultimately drop the case or reject it due to some clerical error, making the entire process pointless. Years of your life can be wasted in a process like this, and the government just doesn't care. They do these kind of things fairly regularly, too. They use the process as the punishment. The stress of courts and judges and charges weighs heavy on a person, like really heavy, and they know that. So, even though they knew they probably couldn’t even win that original criminal case against them, they still wanted to use those charges as a form of punishment. So, fighting back at the government like this is the story of David and Goliath. Not only were these two penetration testers the first ever to be wrongfully arrested for penetration testing, but they're also the first two to ever sue the government to protect their rights as penetration testers. This is an epic story. This case could set a precedent. JUSTIN: It was just the right thing to do, I think. We didn't have a choice, I mean, to have our counter-sue back at them. It was the only way to try to restore any sliver of justice around our case and that state. So, in our minds, it didn't even cross it. Just a no-brainer; had to sue back. But the funny — like David and Goliath, I think that’s hackers, right? It’s like the power that one individual can hold is why governments can be so scared of these individuals. You can do a lot even as a single person. So, against the government, it is a mighty entity, but still, again, that’s kinda for our lawyer to handle. GABBY: It’s all about the information, and we have all of it. JACK: He felt like he had no choice and that was the right thing to do. Wow, those are some powerful words. This is what patriotism looks like in practice, to put the government in check when it overreaches and force it back. So, how does the county react to this? Of course they delay it. Their original court date was supposed to be in 2020, but that got delayed, cancelled, pushed back again and again. The county tried to distance themselves from this in every way possible. They tried to slither out of it, hoping that Justin and Gabby would grow tired or forget about this or just give up. GABBY: The further they could get away from the moment, the better for them, because they wanted it to fall out. They didn't want people to bring it back up. JACK: So, year one goes by. Very little happens. Basically, they spent the whole year just opening the case. Year two goes by. Nothing happens at all. Year three, they just keep delaying things, keep pushing it back, and this is really starting to test Justin and Gabby’s patience. Like, come on, we’ve presented all the evidence to you. Why are you not looking at this case and trying to get it closed? Also, at some point during all that, Chad Leonard, the sheriff that they were upset with, retired and moved out of state entirely. So, whatever outcome this lawsuit’s gonna have, it’s not gonna bother him at all because he’s just relaxing in some Florida community somewhere now. But their lawsuit was with the sheriff’s position, not the sheriff himself, so the case continued. Around this time, too, Justin and Gabby’s relationship with Coalfire started to sour. They didn't feel like they were getting paid enough or treated right by them. GABBY: The first year after we got arrested, we had over $5 million come in directly of people saying, hey, we want to work with Gary and Justin, and we want to work with the Iowa team, and blah, blah, blah. JUSTIN: I think. GABBY: We don't care. JUSTIN: Our story was one of the most valuable things that happened to Coalfire. Even the CEO recognized, yeah, the number-one reason Coalfire is known is because of this case. It is funny; if we ever talk to anybody and we mention, oh, we work at Coalfire — like, oh man, you ever hear that crazy story of those guys that got arrested? I’m like, no, tell me about that. JACK: Gabby quit her job at Coalfire and went to apply at other places. [To guests] I didn't quite get the full picture. Is Coalfire good or bad? GABBY: Individuals at Coalfire are very bad. I think Coalfire as an entity during that time was good. JACK: She was able to quickly get interviews at other places, but even though she was the best for her job and the most qualified, her reputation from this case alone made people turn her down. She had a hard time finding another penetration-testing job because of this story with the Iowa courthouse. She took six months off just to clear her head and relax. GABBY: Like, really started to come into question; like, damn, am I even gonna be able to keep doing this because of what happened? JUSTIN: Great opportunity to start your own business, then, and do it on your own terms. GABBY: Right? Yeah. JUSTIN: Yeah. GABBY: Justin and I had actually talked about it multiple times in the past about starting something different and doing things a little bit differently and treating… JACK: Starting something new yourself. GABBY: Yeah, and just building a company that treats people the way that we thought they should be treated. We had a vision of — we wanted to do things a little bit differently, and so, we did that with Kaiju. JACK: Thus, Kaiju Security was born, a fresh, new penetration-testing company based near Seattle, Washington. GABBY: Adversarial simulation offensive security. JACK: Gabby started it with another guy named Marcus, and Justin moved on to the team shortly after it was formed. After getting this new company started up, the lawsuit was finally making some movement in year five. JUSTIN: Yeah, recently in 2025 it was about showtime. So, then we started getting hot and heavy with it, doing depositions, getting things on record, getting prep for the trial case. So, we were definitely shaping up — yeah, go show up in court. Again, going back to the hacker community, we had some great people like Deviant, Andrew Porter, that agreed to testify in our case just as expert witnesses. So, yeah, we're going through. We really thought we were gonna end up in court. We started getting presented with options to settle pretty quickly. I mean, they wait to the last minute with everything like that. They were throwing out low-ball numbers. I think they had like — just about like our bond or bail is what they first wanted to offer, like $50k. GABBY: Yeah, $50,000. JACK: Okay, so, the county didn't want to go to trial and did want to settle this, but their offer was for $50,000 each, the amount that they paid to get out on bail. $50,000 each, that doesn't even cover their lawyer fees that they spent trying to clear their names. What an insult. So, no, of course they didn't take $50,000 each. They needed more. GABBY: So, we ended up going through arbitration where they take a former judge and — goes back and forth and tries to settle the case. But at that time they were still being super, super, super stingy. They were like, oh, we’ll give them fifty. Then so, the judge, TLDR — the judge comes by to us, and through the entire process — it took all day long — comes to us and goes, I don't think in my entire career I’ve ever seen a case so clear cut as this. This isn't a matter of if you win. This is a matter of how much money you're gonna get. So, I’m gonna go back and I’m gonna beat these guys up pretty good, and he leaves. Marty looks at us and is like, I’ve been doing this for fifty years or something like that, or forty-two years, and he’s like, I have never heard an arbitrator say that ever. I’ve never — not only had he never heard it; he’d never heard of anyone else saying that an arbitrator had said that. So, that was the point, I think, that our confidence started to go like this, 'cause he had seen all of our — everything that we had, and he was just like, yeah, no, this isn't — I don't think this is up for debate. JACK: But even with that, the county stayed silent. Instead, they set a trial date, which was three months away, again making them wait more. So, they prepared for trial. They spent an enormous amount of time and energy to gather their materials, find bodycam footage, get testimonies and depositions and bring in expert witnesses. They even took time off work to go attend this trial, and they booked their flights and their tickets, and they were ready to go. Let me just emphasize what the odds are in this situation. Over 95% of wrongful arrest lawsuits are thrown out due to qualified immunity. Of the few that make it through, 95% of those usually get closed with a zero-dollar settlement, or the government wins at trial. For them to receive more than $50,000 from this lawsuit is about the same odds as hitting the lottery. It’s extremely rare to sue the government over wrongful arrest and win a substantial amount of money. Usually in those situations, it’s because the person was in jail for weeks or months under the wrongful arrest. So, it’s even more rare for someone to spend just one night in jail and get a large settlement offer. In those situations, you would have to prove without a doubt the government conducted an egregious violation, which is what Justin and Gabby was saying happened. [Music] But then a few days before the trial was due to begin, in February 2026, they got a new settlement offer from the county. The county was offering them $600,000 total, $300,000 for each of them, and this was actually the lowest that they would accept, so they took it. The lawsuit was closed. They got paid. They won. This allowed them to celebrate. JUSTIN: Still, I think the biggest one for the community is now we have better precedent, right? So, before, we were just arrested. Felony charges — okay, cops can just arrest pen testers doing their job and try to put them in prison for seven years. But now we can look back, and if that’s ever happening in real time to other testers out there — hey, sir, let’s just take this slow. Take your time. Fully cooperative. But if you want to research, this has happened before, and it’s probably not a good idea to try to prosecute or put me in jail for doing my job. Look what happens. Or the county could have to pay out or — yeah. So, really good to have the win under our belt for the community. GABBY: Everybody else, yeah. I’m obviously much more selfish than Justin is. JACK: Now, finally they can go back to their normal lives feeling like justice has been restored in the best way it possibly can be. Now they're focusing on building Kaiju Security all with a new feather in their cap. JUSTIN: I love saying that, too, 'cause I fought the law and the law won. No, man, the law fought us and we won. JACK: [Outro music] A big thank-you to Justin Wynn and Gabby DeMercurio for reaching out and finding the time to share this story with us. I really like these two, and I look forward to the next time I meet them. Hey, I just launched a new show. It’s called Low. It’s a five-part series. It’s the most crazy story I’ve ever heard, and right now it’s hidden within the Darknet Diaries premium feed. If you want to listen to it early, please go to plus.darknetdiaries.com. Otherwise you're gonna have to wait for the public release, which is coming later this month. This show is created by me, pony pie, Jack Rhysider, mixing by Proximity Sound, and our theme music is by the mysterious Breakmaster Cylinder. There’s an option in WhatsApp, and I can never figure out; is it mark as read or mark as read? This is Darknet Diaries.
